summary:
Russia presents severe legal and physical risks for transgender visitors, and the situation has deteriorated sharply since 2022. Legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care were banned outright in 2023, when Putin signed the law prohibiting gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents; the Supreme Court has designated the "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation; and the expanded "propaganda" law criminalises any public expression — including, explicitly, anything "justifying" gender transition. Foreigners who violate these laws face arrest, up to 15 days' detention, and deportation, and official national government warnings explicitly tell LGBT travellers of this. These statutes apply in every region, including Stavropol Krai.

The UK Home Office country policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) singles out the North Caucasus as the exception to its otherwise non-persecutory finding on Russia: trans people and public LGBT+ advocates in the region are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution. The same note records systematic regional campaigns against LGBT people between 2017 and 2024, and states that the 2023 "extremist" designation carries 2 to 6 years' imprisonment, rising to 6 to 10 years for organising.

David Isteev of North Caucasus SOS, interviewed by the Human Rights House Foundation, states that there is no safe life for LGBTIQ+ people in the North Caucasus and that even private existence can trigger violence, detention or forced return to families. Speaking as a regional defender in exile, he reports year-on-year deterioration across the region.

Global Affairs Canada's Russia advisory tells all travellers to avoid all travel, and names the Stavropol region among the areas subject to frequent terrorist attacks, alongside Chechnya, Dagestan and Ingushetia. The same advisory warns that 2SLGBTQI+ persons and members of their families who advocate for them have been attacked, harassed and abused, that since January 2024 advocacy organisations have been treated as "extremist", and that foreigners are under surveillance.

Entry into certain areas requires special permission from the Ministry of Interior: the advisory's list covers Kabardino-Balkaria (including Elbrus), Karachai-Cherkessia and North Ossetia. Stavropol Krai does not appear on that permission list, but the avoid-all-travel warning, the terrorist-attack risk and the surveillance warning apply to entry into the krai itself, and the permission regime restricts onward movement through the neighbouring territories a visitor would transit.
tangentialFactors:
Stavropol Krai is an administrative krai rather than one of the North Caucasus republics, and the most extreme documented violence in the region — secret prisons, purges, coerced conscription — is Chechen-specific. The legal exposure a visitor faces in Stavropol Krai nonetheless derives from the national statutes, which have no regional carve-out.

The UK Home Office position is a comparison worth holding: its June 2025 note finds no general persecution basis for LGBT+ asylum claims from Russia, but carves out the North Caucasus. A trans visitor therefore faces a materially different assessment of risk in this territory than in Moscow or St Petersburg, where the documented pattern is raids, fines and extremism charges rather than the regional campaigns recorded between 2017 and 2024.

Enforcement volume nationally is rising: Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions for alleged participation in the designated "international LGBT movement" or for displaying its alleged symbols as of 30 June 2025, and Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that propaganda-law cases have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, with fines bringing more than 60 million rubles into the state budget over two years.

The speed of the post-designation crackdown is documented: The Guardian reported on 17 January 2024 that within 48 hours of the Supreme Court's ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars, with about 100 patrons at one venue ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, and at least two other venues raided the same night.
localsOnly:
Residents of Stavropol Krai live under the same 2023 ban on legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care as the rest of Russia, so no route to updated documents or medical transition exists locally.

Advocacy organisations have been treated as "extremist" since January 2024, which exposes anyone associated with LGBT advocacy, and anyone displaying alleged symbols, to administrative and criminal charges. The 2023 designation of the "international LGBT movement" carries 2 to 6 years' imprisonment, and 6 to 10 years for organising.

Regional defenders report that even private existence can trigger violence, detention or forced return to families, and that conditions have worsened year on year. In December 2024 the Associated Press reported that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

Physical coercion against transgender people is documented in the wider national context: BBC Russian (27 July 2024) followed "Ada", a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping.

The UK Home Office country policy note affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: the sources do not state whether the UK Home Office's North Caucasus exception, drafted around the North Caucasus republics, is applied to Stavropol Krai by name. The krai borders the region and is named in the Canadian advisory's terrorist-attack list, but the inventory contains no explicit finding extending the persecution exception to this territory.

Unresolved: the earlier framing of Stavropol Krai as covered by the Canadian special-permission requirement is not supported by the retrieved advisory text, whose permission list is Kabardino-Balkaria (including Elbrus), Karachai-Cherkessia and North Ossetia. Stavropol appears in that advisory only in the terrorist-attack enumeration.

Not sourced: any claim about enforcement in the south-eastern districts bordering Chechnya, including security-and-customs practice there. No source in the inventory addresses district-level enforcement within the krai.

The US State Department advisory for Russia remains Level 4, Do Not Travel, with warnings directed at LGBT travellers; no Stavropol-specific US guidance is in the inventory.
